title: VB9-08459
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appeal is allowed. For the following reasons, I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.
XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of Nigeria. He alleges that he fears persecution in Nigeria because he is a bisexual man.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected the Appellant's claim because it determined that he failed to provide sufficient reliable and trustworthy evidence to support his allegations. The Appellant claims the RPD made several errors, including in its credibility assessment of the Appellant's evidence regarding his sexual orientation.

I have conducted an independent assessment of the appeal and consulted the Chairperson's Guideline 9 - Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression1 (SOGIE Guideline). I find that the RPD erred in its credibility assessment of the Appellant's evidence regarding his past same-sex relationship and sexual orientation. In my view, the Appellant has credibly established his sexual orientation, on a balance of probabilities. I also find that the Appellant has established his risk of harm in Nigeria because same-sex relationships are illegal in Nigeria. Therefore, I find that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. ANALYSIS Role of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD)
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2 Merits of the Appeal The RPD erred in its credibility assessment
I find that the RPD erred when it determined that the Appellant failed to provide sufficient reliable and trustworthy evidence to support his allegation that he is a bisexual man.

The Appellant alleges the RPD erred because it relied on preconceived expectations regarding the amount of self-reflection he should have done regarding his sexual orientation. The Appellant also alleges the RPD erred because it used these expectations to assess whether or not he provided an adequate level of detail in his evidence to credibly establish his sexual orientation.

In its reasons the RPD characterized the Appellant's testimony as superficial, shallow, sparse and lacking in detail on his sexuality, his boyfriend and their relationship.3 Based on these findings, the RPD concluded that there was insufficient meaningful testimony to accept the Appellant's sexual identity claims on a balance of probabilities.4

The RPD also stated that "While there is no uniform trajectory, coming out stories are epiphany for sexual minorities, it is reasonable to expect individuals to have reflected on their nonconforming sexuality, particularly in a country where it is not only highly taboo, but also highly criminalized." 5 The RPD went on to state that "The claimant, however, lacked any self-reflection, awareness, or emotion about his sexual identity."6

I have reviewed the documentary evidence and listened to the audio recording of the Appellant's testimony before the RPD. I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred because it incorrectly relied on pre-conceived notions of sexual identity. In so doing, the RPD focused on the degree to which the Appellant's testimony did not align with the type of testimony the RPD expected to hear rather than on the content of the Appellant's testimony. I find that this resulted in the RPD mischaracterizing the Appellant's evidence.

As discussed below, my independent assessment is that the Appellant provided adequate credible testimony to establish his sexual orientation. In his appeal submissions the Appellant alleges that the RPD made several other errors when it assessed his claim. I have not addressed these other allegations in these reasons because I find that the Appellant's sexual orientation is determinative in this appeal.

In his Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative the Appellant stated that he began to be attracted to men when he was in high school and that he could not explain why he was having sexual and emotional feelings towards males of his own age and older.7 He stated that at the same time he was having the same feelings towards the opposite sex and was confused about his mixed feelings.8

In his BOC, the Appellant also stated that he met XXXX XXXX who was a bisexual friend from his community. He stated that they were attracted to each other and that XXXX would take him to movies and shopping and that he lured him into bisexuality.9 The Appellant stated that in 2014 his cousin caught him and XXXX making love and told their extended family about the Appellant's relationship.10 The Appellant claims that he could not begin his studies at the XXXX XXXX XXXX in Nigeria because he had been outed and feared he would be found and arrested because homosexual relationships are illegal in Nigeria.

Therefore, the Appellant left for South Africa to continue his studies in 2015. He stated in his BOC that he could be open about his sexual orientation in South Africa and that he explored his sexuality freely while there. However, he stated that he fled South Africa after he suffered a xenophobic attack in 2016. The Appellant continued his studies in Kenya, but soon left Kenya because he could not openly practice bisexuality in Kenya and he feared being deported to Nigeria. He stated in his BOC that in 2017 he travelled to the United States and then came to Canada to seek refugee protection.

During the RPD hearing the Appellant elaborated on the information he provided in his BOC regarding his sexual orientation and past same-sex relationship. In my view, the Appellant's BOC narrative and testimony before the RPD were credible and provided adequate information regarding: his personal feelings about his sexual orientation growing up; his first homosexual encounter; how his sexual orientation was discovered; how his family members reacted to his sexual orientation; and his exploration of his sexual orientation in South Africa to credibly establish that he is a bisexual man, on a balance of probabilities.

The RPD Member asked the Appellant about his first sexual experience which was with a man. The Appellant testified that this experience was with a friend who had been showing him signs, like the way he had been appreciating him the same way a guy would appreciate a lady by saying things like "you look good", "I like you".11 The Appellant stated that at that time he started to suspect that his friend was attracted to him.12

The Appellant testified that on his first date with this friend they went to see a romantic movie at night. He stated that his friend touched him on his penis in the dark movie theatre and that he responded, that they had been drinking alcohol together and that they went back to his apartment and had sex. The Appellant testified that after this encounter they started dating and had a relationship that lasted two years from 2012 to 2014.13 He testified that they did not break up but lost contact because they both fled the area of Nigeria they were in after they were discovered.

The Appellant testified that in 2013 he began a long-distance relationship with a woman. When asked by the RPD Member whether she knew he was bisexual, the Appellant sated that he did not tell her about his bisexuality because it was illegal in Nigeria but that his same-sex partner knew about his girlfriend.14

The Appellant testified that in South Africa he went to gay clubs and parties freely but that he never had a relationship in South Africa. He also testified that he chose to study in South Africa because his sexual orientation was not illegal there. The RPD Member asked him to describe the clubs he went to in South Africa. At first the Appellant responded that he did not understand the question. He then stated that they were normal clubs like every other club because they are legal. He said that they are like the clubs on XXXX XXXX. The RPD Member again asked how they are different from other clubs. The Appellant testified that when you go there you will see men kissing and that there was gay art on the walls.15

The Appellant testified that when his mother found out about his sexual orientation she was disappointed and cried but that she forgave him. However, the other members of his family rejected him because of his sexual orientation.16 He stated that people who are gay in Nigeria face persecution, rejection and live in fear. He testified that when he was growing up he learned that homosexuals are people of destruction, that it is against Christianity. He said that when he started feeling attracted to men he was scared, he did not know how his life was going to turn out, and that if people found out he would be in serious trouble and that there was no one to talk to because everyone was against it.17 He said that he thought he should have the right to be who he wants to be and that he felt he should not have to live in fear.

The SOGIE Guideline provides guidance on how sexual orientation allegations should be assessed by the Board. The guideline states that the assessment of credibility may be more difficult in a claim involving sexual orientation. For example, while an individual's experiences and behaviors related to their SOGIE may be expressed in private and public spheres, an individual's testimony may be the only evidence of their SOGIE, and it may be difficult for an individual to provide testimony regarding their sexual orientation and sexual history given the personal nature of the information. In light of this guidance, I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant's evidence demonstrates that he was previously in a same-sex relationship and is a bisexual man. Risk of Harm in Nigeria

The documentary evidence is clear that same-sex relationships are illegal in Nigeria. As a result, there is no state protection for bisexuals such as the Appellant in Nigeria.18 Multiple sources indicate that members of the LGBTQ+ community are ostracized by Nigerian society and face a serious possibility of persecution by the police and the general public. This persecution may include harassment, violence, discrimination, imprisonment and the death penalty based on sexual orientation, and is corroborated by the Appellant's testimony.19

Based on the national documentation and the Appellant's evidence, I find that there is a serious possibility of the Appellant being persecuted in Nigeria because of his sexual orientation. As a result, I find that the Appellant is a Convention refugees under s. 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The appeal is allowed. The RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.
